items.body: Live and batch recorders, audio and video import, and a choice of transcription engines: Apple on-device, Whisper, or Parakeet. Every recording lands in your daily document, with playback you can click straight into. The direct build can also type finished phrases into the app you are already using.

items.body: A voice recorder for when you are away from the desk. Live dictation, a dictation board that collects what you capture, and your transcripts and audio files kept close. Transcription runs on-device with Apple Speech.

liveEdit.lead: Wrong word? Wrong line? Edit or remove it while you are still recording. No need to wait for a finished take.

voiceExamples.heading: Additional layers of control over what gets written
voiceExamples.intro: Recognition is never perfect, so SpeakWith adds a few of its own on top of the engine. Each one decides a little more of what actually reaches the page.
voiceExamples.lead: Some terms come back wrong every time you say them, usually names and jargon. Record a few readings of one and SpeakWith keeps them as reference sound. Each example shows what the engine actually heard. That gives SpeakWith more ways to spot the word, and shows you whether one it keeps missing can be corrected at all.

item.caption: Add the term, record a few readings, and see what each one was heard as.
item.ariaLabel: The SpeakWith Voice Examples pane: a list of special terms on the left, the term Nguyen selected on the right, each recorded example showing a Heard as line beneath it, and a Record Example button.

methods.title: Special terms
methods.body: Some words are not spelled the way they sound. Worcestershire is one. List the names and jargon you rely on and live dictation watches for them, widening how each one can be matched so it survives more than one pronunciation. Others are harder still: Siobhan is spelled by Irish rules rather than English ones, so its letters do not map onto English sounds at all. For those you can point a spoken cue at the word instead and say Sierra Bravo to write it. Every substitution that fired is listed in a report.

methods.title: Hallucination gate
methods.body: Voice detection on its own cannot always tell a breath from a word, and a recognizer handed one can return a word you never said, sometimes a Yeah or an Okay. The gate waits for the written text, then blocks activations that were never meant as speech. New filler goes on the block list as you meet it, so it stops reaching the page.

moat.title: Your recordings stay on your Mac. Plain files, no account.

items.label: Local
items.body: Your recordings never leave your Mac. Optional session titles can run on a local Ollama model or your own OpenAI key, and only when you switch them on. A separate optional correction check can ask OpenAI to vet flagged lines.

items.label: Markdown
items.body: A plain .md file on disk. Open it in VS Code, Obsidian, or any editor. Feed it to any tool.

items.label: No account
items.body: No login. No subscription cloud. No data trade.

items.label: On your computer
items.body: Transcription and summarization run on your Mac. Nothing is uploaded. Ever.

inclusive.heading: You don't have to talk to AI to use this.
inclusive.p1: SpeakWith works on its own. Speak, get a clean markdown file, then edit it, search its text, and share it. Keep it that way for as long as you like.
inclusive.p2Html: The file is also something you can hand to an AI when you decide that's useful. AI is a thing the file can do, not a thing you have to do.

items.title: A document for every day
items.body: Everything you record or type on a given day flows into a single organised document, in the order it happened. Tomorrow, a fresh one begins.

items.title: Type into app
items.body: Turn on the switch in the live recorder, or set a hotkey in Settings. SpeakWith types each finished phrase into the app with focus. Available in the direct (Gumroad) Mac build.

items.title: Bring in audio & video
items.body: Drop in a voice memo, a recorded call, or a screen recording. SpeakWith writes it up and folds it into your daily document like anything else.

items.title: Session titles, local or cloud
items.body: Name each dictation session from its transcript. Pick OpenAI or a local Ollama model under Settings, Session AI. Generate stays in the AI sidebar when you want a heading.

items.title: Speak and keep working
items.body: Speaking and working no longer take turns. Your dictation flows into the document on its own, so you can organise sections, paste in snippets, or type something completely different at the same time, without interrupting the words you're capturing.

items.title: Speaking rhythm, on screen
items.body: A live meter shows the pauses inside what you are saying. Over time, that quiet feedback shapes how you speak: you hold a topic together longer, and the text on the other end gets easier to work with.

parallel.heading: Like having an extra pair of hands
parallel.p1Html: Most tools force you to shift your focus from thinking to operating an application. SpeakWith removes that friction. Every recorder lives in the same application, and what you capture writes out to the project you have selected.
parallel.p2: You can control SpeakWith with a remote microphone, so you never need to touch the keyboard, and there is no key to remember before you start recording. On the direct build, turn on the recorder switch or a hotkey and speak into the app you are already in.

rhythm.heading: The longer you use it, the better you speak.
rhythm.p1: While you record, a small meter shows the pauses inside what you are saying. Over weeks, the effect adds up. You notice when a thought starts to fragment, you stay on a topic a beat longer, and the next time you do it a little more cleanly.
rhythm.p2: The text on the other end changes too. Single topics arrive in coherent pieces, and paragraphs hold together, so your daily document is something you can hand to a person or a tool without reshaping it first.

homebase.eyebrow: Built for how real work happens
homebase.heading: The home base your thinking returns to
homebase.p1: Real work runs in parallel. You start something that takes time to come back: a long process, a tool working away, a task you've handed off. Instead of waiting, you begin the next thing, then another. Before long, several are in flight at once.
homebase.p2: Tools come and go; your daily document stays. It is the one place that holds every thread in a single file that is yours: what each one is for, where you left it, what to check when it lands. You can keep many things moving at once because you are not holding them all in your head.

items.q: Does SpeakWith need an internet connection?
items.a: No. Recording, transcription, organising your daily document, and searching its text all happen on your Mac. SpeakWith does its core work offline.

items.q: Can the optional AI features run locally?
items.a: Session titles can. Choose Ollama under Settings, Session AI, and titles stay on your Mac. Correction checks, if you enable them, use your OpenAI key. Core recording and transcription never need the network.

items.q: Where are my recordings and documents stored?
items.a: As ordinary files on your Mac. You can open, copy, back up, and delete them with any tool you like. They are not locked inside the app or held in an account.

Automatic transcription is very good but never perfect. Names and specialist terms are the usual places small errors appear. Your daily document is fully editable, so treat the transcript as an excellent first draft you can correct.
items.moreLabel: See how the recorder reports your correction rate.

items.q: Does using SpeakWith change how I speak?
items.a: It can, through quiet feedback. While you record, a small meter shows the pauses inside what you are saying, something you can glance at without breaking your train of thought. Over weeks, you may hold a topic together longer and let it land in a single, coherent piece. Your daily document gets easier to work with, and so can the way you speak to people away from the screen.

items.q: Can I import audio and video I already have?
items.a: Yes. Import a voice memo, a recorded meeting, or a screen recording, and SpeakWith writes it up the same way it writes up a live recording.

items.q: Can I keep working while a recording is written up?
items.a: Yes. That is one of SpeakWith's best features. Type and paste into the day's document while dictation is still processing; everything ends up in the correct chronological order.

items.q: Can I dictate into other apps?
items.a: Yes, on the direct (Gumroad) Mac build. Turn on the recorder switch, or set a hotkey in Settings. SpeakWith types each finished phrase into whichever app currently has keyboard focus. Your daily document still receives everything as usual. The sandboxed App Store build cannot do this; macOS does not allow cross-app typing from sandboxed apps.

It's on the way, and it will be free. SpeakWith for iOS is a companion voice recorder: live dictation, a dictation board that collects what you capture, and your transcripts and audio files on hand. It transcribes on-device with Apple Speech, and it works alongside the Mac app rather than replacing it.

items.q: On iOS, the permission prompt says speech is "sent to Apple". Is my voice uploaded?
items.a: No. That line is Apple's standard wording for the speech-recognition permission, shown to every app that asks for it. SpeakWith transcribes on-device using Apple's built-in dictation: your audio is turned into text on your iPhone or iPad. The only thing that downloads is the speech model itself, once. After that, transcription runs on your device.
English today. Support for more languages is in development, and they will arrive in updates as they are ready.

It is a voice recorder. SpeakWith is tuned for speech and dictation, the way a person actually talks, so it does its best work on the human voice. It is not built for capturing music or ambient sound.

items.q: Is the Mac download signed and checked by Apple?
items.a: Yes. The direct Mac download is signed with our Apple Developer ID, so the apps you install match the build we shipped. Before upload, Apple's notary service scans that submission for known malicious software and for code-signing problems, and we staple the ticket so Gatekeeper can check it. That scan is not an App Store review, and it is not a promise that the software is free of malware.

automation.heading: Automation
automation.intro: SpeakWith has two recorders you can drive from outside the app: Live dictation (real-time, finalised at each pause) and Live audio (voice-activated). You can start, stop, and control either one from the command line, a macOS Shortcut, Automator, or a hotkey launcher — with no extra setup. There are two equivalent ways to send a command: the speakwith:// URL scheme (simplest) and AppleScript (for scripting environments that prefer it).

paragraphs.text:
The fastest way to begin a take is the URL scheme — one line any shell can run. Start the Live dictation recorder:

open "speakwith://live-dictation/start"

Prefer AppleScript? This does the same thing:

osascript -e 'tell application "SpeakWith" to start recording recorder live dictation'

Start the Live audio (voice-activated) recorder instead:

open "speakwith://batch/start"

Stop the current take (the microphone stays powered on, ready to start again):

open "speakwith://live-dictation/stop"

Each recorder supports ten actions. The table below shows the Live dictation recorder. For the Live audio recorder, replace “live dictation” with “batch” in the AppleScript command, and “live-dictation” with “batch” in the URL, with one exception, noted under the table. Two further commands control typing into other apps and name no recorder at all; they have their own section below.

ActionAppleScript commandURL scheme
Power on (microphone only)power on recorder live dictationspeakwith://live-dictation/power-on
Power off (release the microphone)power off recorder live dictationspeakwith://live-dictation/power-off
Start a takestart recording recorder live dictationspeakwith://live-dictation/start
Start a take, keeping the words in SpeakWithstart recording in app recorder live dictationspeakwith://live-dictation/start-in-app
Stop a takestop recording recorder live dictationspeakwith://live-dictation/stop
Set standby on / offset standby recorder live dictation enabled true (or false)speakwith://live-dictation/standby?on=true (or false)
Toggle power (flip the microphone)toggle power recorder live dictationspeakwith://live-dictation/toggle-power
Toggle recording (flip the take, microphone stays on)toggle recording recorder live dictationspeakwith://live-dictation/toggle
Toggle standbytoggle standby recorder live dictationspeakwith://live-dictation/toggle-standby
Bring the app forward and show the recorderfocus recorder live dictationspeakwith://live-dictation/focus

The three toggle actions flip whatever the recorder is doing right now. They take no on or off argument: the recorder’s current state is the argument, read at the moment the command arrives. That is what lets a single hotkey mean both start and stop. They sit at different levels: toggle power holds or releases the microphone, toggle recording starts or ends a take with the microphone kept on, and toggle standby flips level mode.

“In app” means in SpeakWith. If you have turned on typing into other apps, start-in-app turns it back off before the take begins, so your words land in SpeakWith rather than in whatever window happens to be in front. Plain start leaves that setting exactly as you left it. This is the one action with no Live audio counterpart — the Live audio recorder never types into other apps, so speakwith://batch/start-in-app simply does the same thing as speakwith://batch/start. And on any build that does not offer typing into other apps at all — the Mac App Store build, for one — the two are identical as well.

Focus never touches the microphone. focus brings SpeakWith forward and opens that recorder’s pane, and that is all it does: it does not power the microphone on, start a take, or change the typing-into-other-apps switch. Bind it when you want the recorder in front of you before you decide what to do next. Running it again when SpeakWith is already frontmost changes nothing.
Each AppleScript command runs inside tell application "SpeakWith" to … — for example, osascript -e 'tell application "SpeakWith" to power off recorder batch'.

A few things worth knowing. The directional commands are safe to repeat: running “start” while already recording, or “power on” while already on, simply does nothing. The four toggle commands are the exception, and deliberately so: sending one twice returns you to where you started. Standby only affects the recorder that is currently powered on; it never powers a recorder on by itself.

Typing into other apps is the switch that sends what you say into whatever window is in front, instead of into SpeakWith. Two commands control it. Neither names a recorder: only Live dictation can type elsewhere, so there is nothing to choose.

ActionAppleScript commandURL scheme
Toggle typing into other appstoggle type into appspeakwith://dictation/toggle
Turn typing into other apps onset type into app enabled truespeakwith://dictation/type-into-app?on=true
Turn typing into other apps offset type into app enabled falsespeakwith://dictation/type-into-app?on=false

These do exactly what the in-app switch and the global hotkey do. That includes moving the recorder, not only the setting: turning typing on starts dictating (and if a take is already running, it begins a fresh recording from that point, so the dictated audio is its own file), and turning it off ends that take, unless you have asked SpeakWith to keep recording when typing stops.

toggle flips the switch, so sending it twice returns you to where you started. The two set commands are directional and idempotent: asking for a state you are already in does nothing at all, so a script can assert “typing off” on a timer without ever interrupting a take. Both set forms require you to say which way: set type into app with no enabled, or the URL without ?on=, is refused rather than assumed to mean on.

Turning typing off is not the same as start-in-app. set type into app enabled false only turns the switch off. start-in-app turns it off and starts a take. Bind the first when you want your next words to stay in SpeakWith, the second when you want to start capturing right now.
On builds that do not offer typing into other apps at all, such as the Mac App Store build, all three commands are accepted and do nothing.
By default these commands find SpeakWith by name. If you have more than one SpeakWith build installed, pin the exact one you want by its bundle identifier:
osascript -e 'tell application id "com.ikisystems.speakwith.macos.gumroad" to start recording recorder live dictation'

The shipping bundle identifiers are com.ikisystems.speakwith.macos.gumroad (Gumroad), com.ikisystems.speakwith.macos.appstore (Mac App Store), and com.ikisystems.speakwith.macos (Developer ID direct download).

Because these are ordinary commands and URLs, you can turn any of them into a keyboard shortcut today. Drop one into a macOS Shortcut, an Automator “Run Shell Script” action, or a launcher such as Raycast, Alfred, or Keyboard Maestro, and give it the hotkey you like.

If the hotkey is how you begin dictating, start-in-app is usually the one to bind: it means “capture this here” no matter how you last left the typing-into-other-apps switch.

open "speakwith://live-dictation/start-in-app"

If your launcher would otherwise need a separate “activate the app” step first, focus replaces it: the command brings SpeakWith forward on its own, and it leaves the microphone alone, so a macro can put the recorder in front of you without starting a take.

open "speakwith://live-dictation/focus"

For push-to-dictate into whatever window is in front, bind the typing toggle. One key turns typing on and starts dictating; the same key turns it off again.

open "speakwith://dictation/toggle"

recorderBadge.heading: Reading the recorder badge
recorderBadge.intro: At the left of the record bar on the Mac, SpeakWith shows two short lines in a small monospaced typeface. The first identifies the build you are running. The second tracks your dictation over time. The diagram below walks through each segment.
recorderBadge.diagramAlt: Annotated diagram of the SpeakWith recorder badge. Line one reads SpeakWith 2.14.0 Pro (app=eng 20260923.10): the app name, version, edition, and the build stamp shared by the app and its engine. Line two reads 9,834w, 1,770s, 51,368c, 0.7% wer, 0.1% st: words, sentences, and characters dictated since the last reset, then the share of words you corrected and the share your special terms corrected.

sections.heading: The first line: which build you are running

paragraphs.text: The line starts with the app name, its version, and the edition. The edition reads Pro on a direct download, or MAS if you installed SpeakWith from the Mac App Store.

The part in parentheses is the build stamp: the build date, then the build number for that day. The app and its transcription engine are stamped together, so they normally show one value. If they ever differ, the line shows both, which is the first thing to mention if you write in about a problem.

sections.heading: The second line: your dictation tally

paragraphs.text: The three counts are words, sentences, and characters you have dictated since the last reset, across all sessions. The s stands for sentences, not seconds.

The two percentages use the word count as their denominator. The correction rate (wer) is the share of dictated words you went back and changed, a personal stand-in for WER (Word Error Rate). It only counts corrections you actually made, so the true error rate may be higher. The special-terms rate (st) is the share of words that your own special terms corrected: names, terminology, and words you pronounce your own way, which the recognizer would otherwise get wrong.

There is no visible control on the badge itself; the space belongs to the Record, Flush, and Power buttons. Long-press anywhere on the badge to open the About window. About holds the switch that hides or shows the tally, the reset that starts the counts again from zero, and a correction rate measured on reviewed lines only.
In the app, hover over any segment of the badge to see the same explanation as a tooltip. The values in the diagram are sample values.

seeAlso.label: See also: reading live transcript corrections, the marks on each line as it lands.

statusMonitor.heading: The floating status monitor
statusMonitor.intro: While the live-direct mic is held, SpeakWith can float a small pill above every other window. It shows one colored dot and one or two words: the mode you are in right now. You read it from across the room, or from the corner of your eye while you type in another app, without bringing SpeakWith forward. The diagram below shows the pill, its five modes, and the one thing it cannot replace.
statusMonitor.diagramAlt: Annotated diagram of the SpeakWith floating status monitor: a small rounded pill sitting over another app's window. It carries the SpeakWith mark, a blue dot, the words Type into app, and a smaller detail line reading Into open field. Below it, five smaller pills show the five modes with their colors: Recording in red, Type into app in blue, Voice pull in indigo, Listening in orange, and Monitoring in green, with a note that Listening is level mode and a hardware mute switch pauses and resumes it. A row of check marks reads Menu bar hidden, Dock hidden, SpeakWith in the background. At the bottom, three app icons carry small red Dock badges reading REC, TYPE, and a pause mark, captioned as the fallback.

paragraphs.text: Four things, left to right. The SpeakWith mark, so you know whose badge it is when it is the only thing of ours on screen. A colored dot for the mode. The mode word beside the dot, because a color on its own is easy to misread and the word settles it. And, when there is something to add, a smaller detail line, for example when your words are going into an open text field.

The dot can pulse, fading in and out like the recording light in the sidebar: faster while recording or typing into another app, slower while listening. That is a separate switch, so you can keep the dot solid if a moving light in the corner of your eye is not what you want.

Recording, in red: a take is running and going where it always goes, into your day document. Type into app, in blue: a take is running and being typed into whatever app is in front of you. Voice pull, in indigo: a take is running and a shell client is pulling the words instead. Listening, in orange: level mode standby, with the mic held and a take starting the moment you speak up. Monitoring, in green: the mic is held and metering, with no take running.

Blue against red is the comparison this pill exists to make easy. Before it, recording into your document and typing into another app looked the same from a distance, and finding out which one you were in meant switching to SpeakWith. Now a glance at the pill tells you whether your next sentence lands in your document or in the email you are looking at.

Listening is the mode to know about if your microphone has a hardware mute switch. Level mode watches the audio level rather than a button, so flipping the mute switch drops the level and pauses the recorder, and flipping it back resumes. No key, no click, no window to find: the orange dot tells you SpeakWith is waiting, and the pill going red tells you it heard you.

When more than one applies, the pill shows the one that matters most: Voice pull first, then Type into app, then Recording. It appears only in live-direct dictation. Batch capture, and the mic being off, show no pill at all.

sections.heading: Nothing else to keep on screen

paragraphs.text: The pill is its own small window. It takes no slot in the menu bar, needs no Dock, and never takes keyboard focus, so it cannot steal a keystroke from the app you are typing into. You can hide the menu bar and the Dock, put SpeakWith in the background, fill the screen with the app you are working in, and the pill is still there.

Drag it anywhere once and it stays put, on top of everything, until you power the mic off. Many people park it in a corner next to where their words are landing, so the mode and the text sit in one glance.

sections.heading: If you keep the Dock showing

paragraphs.text: The Dock badge is the fallback. SpeakWith's Dock icon reads REC while recording, TYPE while typing into another app, and a pause mark while listening in level mode. It is there whether or not the pill is, and it is enough if your Dock is always visible and you only need to know that a take is running.

What it cannot do is color-code the modes: macOS paints every Dock badge the same red, whatever the word inside it. That is the reason the floating monitor exists, and the reason it, not the badge, is the one to reach for when you type into other apps.

Settings, Dictation, under Type into app: Show mode indicator floats the pill; Pulse the mode indicator makes the dot breathe. Both are in the direct-download builds of SpeakWith. The Mac App Store build keeps the Dock badge.

seeAlso.label: See also: reading the recorder badge, the two lines at the left of the record bar.

liveTranscriptCorrections.heading: Reading live transcript corrections
liveTranscriptCorrections.intro: Once a line of live dictation settles, SpeakWith can mark it in two ways. Inside the line, color and underlines show which words you changed yourself. After the line, small badges show what SpeakWith corrected on its own and, if you have switched them on, what its extra checks found. Most lines carry no marks at all. The diagram below shows one line with every kind of mark on it.
liveTranscriptCorrections.diagramAlt: Annotated diagram of one settled live dictation line in SpeakWith, a portrait photographer's note between sittings. The line reads: Edit the first three headshots, then call Aaliyah before Okafor's sitting. The word first is struck through and faded because it was deleted. The word three is in the typed-words color over a pale band because it was typed in to replace tree. The words then call sit on a pale band with a dotted underline because they were dictated into the line. The word headshots is plain because the recognizer wrote it. Three badges trail the text: a Special Terms rewrite reading alia to Aaliyah, a Voice Examples correction reading Akheffer to Okafor, and a green check mark from the second pass.

paragraphs.text: The line you see is not always the line you spoke. You can open any settled line and fix it with the keyboard, or dictate a phrase straight into it, and the day document keeps the result. Playback, though, still plays the original audio. So each word is painted by where it came from, and the words the recognizer wrote stay plain.

MarkWhat it means
Typed wordsYour typed-words color, over a pale band of the same hue. If you said three headshots and the line came back as tree headshots, opening it and typing three marks only three.
Dictated into a lineThe text keeps its normal color, sits on a pale band of the spoken-into-line color, and takes a dotted underline in a complementary shade. Open a line, speak a phrase, and the phrase lands marked this way.
Deleted wordsStill visible, struck through and faded, like tracked changes in a word processor. A line you removed entirely is struck through as a whole and dimmed.
Plain wordsThe recognizer wrote them and nobody changed them. No color, no band.

Both colors are yours to choose under Settings, Playback: Typed words and Spoken-into-line. The band and the dotted underline are derived from the color you pick, so the two families stay distinct at a glance.
Only your own edits are painted. When SpeakWith joins two spans into one sentence, or a second engine re-reads a line, those words were all spoken, so they stay plain.

sections.heading: Badges after the line: corrections SpeakWith made

paragraphs.text: A badge trails the text of the line it belongs to. There is no reserved column, so a line with nothing to report looks exactly like every other line. When several corrections land on one line, they share a badge, separated by commas. Hover over any badge to read a full explanation.

BadgeMeaning
↦ alia → AaliyahA rewrite from your Special Terms list. The first arrow marks the list, and the second reads heard, then written: the recognizer wrote alia, and your rule for the name Aaliyah replaced it. This layer is always on: the badge appears whenever a listed term was rewritten, whatever mode the recorder is in.
Akheffer → OkaforThe term spotter heard one of your special terms in the audio and corrected the line to match. The arrow means the text changed.
NguyenThe spotter heard a term but the line was not changed: usually the term was already spelled correctly, or correcting is switched off. The tooltip says which.
⚡ Akheffer → OkaforThe match came from one of your Voice Examples, a recording of you saying the name, rather than from its spelling. The bolt is reserved for that. Okafor is the kind of name that earns one: no spelling rule covers how it is misheard.

The spotter is set up under Settings, Corrections. Show spotted special terms hangs the badge on every line where a term was heard. Correct spotted special terms in the line lets the spotter change the text, and a badge with an arrow appears whenever it does, so a correction never lands silently.

One more check can run on each line. It is off by default and lives under Settings, Debug, because it is for understanding the engines rather than for everyday dictation. When it is on, one more glyph trails the line.

The second pass re-reads short lines with a second engine and reports with a single character.

GlyphMeaning
…Queued. The second engine reads the line again once the take stops.
✓Green. The second engine heard the same words.
≠The second engine heard something different. A row appears beneath the line with the other reading, so you can compare the two.
?Orange. The second engine returned nothing, or could not read the audio. Its model may be missing or still loading.
The switch is Show second-pass diagnostics. It never changes what is written. It only shows what happened.

An unmarked line is the normal case, and it can mean several things. The recognizer got the line right and nobody changed it. A special term was already spelled correctly, so there was nothing to correct. Or the second pass is simply switched off, so its glyph draws nothing.
If you expected a correction and see no badge, check the two spotter switches under Settings, Corrections first, then that the term is in your Special Terms list or has a Voice Example.

seeAlso.label: See also: reading the recorder badge, which reports your correction rate over time.

sendToAgent.heading: Send to agent
sendToAgent.intro: Send to agent takes the topics you have checked in the Outline and hands them, as one message, to a coding agent running on your Mac. The agent is connected over ACP, the Agent Client Protocol, and that connection is what lets SpeakWith ask the agent which folder to work in and which model to use, so you choose both from a menu instead of typing them. This page follows one job from the Outline through to the message the agent receives.
sendToAgent.diagramAlt: Annotated diagram of the two panels behind Send to agent in SpeakWith. The upper panel is the Destination block from the Agent tab: three labelled rows reading Agent, Project, and Model, each with a pop-up menu, and an Add folder button beside Project. Beneath it the Project menu is shown opened, with a Recent section listing folders and when they were last used, and an All projects section listing the rest. The lower panel is the program block of Settings under Agent: an Agent program row showing a file path with a Change button and a small minus, an Arguments text field, and a Project folder row showing a folder path with the same Change button and minus. Numbered callouts name each control.

paragraphs.text: You need one coding agent installed on this Mac, such as Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, or Gemini. If you use a session manager that publishes its projects to SpeakWith, have it running. That is all. If the agent you want is not one SpeakWith finds on its own, see Point SpeakWith at a program of your own, near the end of this page.

sections.heading: The job

paragraphs.text: This morning you dictated a session about chapter 4 of a book. The manuscript lives in a folder named lighthouse-book. Two Outline rows belong in that chapter. A third row, The lamp oil, stays unchecked.

sections.figureAlt: The Outline with three rows. The storm scene and Names to keep have filled circles. Names to keep says the keeper is Mara Voss. The lamp oil has an empty circle and is not sent.

sections.heading: Send checked topics to an agent

paragraphs.text: Destination is already set in the figure at the top of this page. On that same tab, the two topics, the instruction, and Send to agent sit together.

sections.figureAlt: The Agent tab, ready to send. The status line reads Claude Code, lighthouse-book, default model. A caption says 2 topics will be sent as one prompt turn. Preview tiles show The storm scene and Names to keep. The instruction names chapters/04-the-storm.md and forbids a new character. A blue Send to agent button is under that box. Callouts name the status line, the caption, Optional instruction, and the button.

steps.title: Check the topics.
steps.text: In the Outline, tick each topic you want the agent to see. Until at least one is checked, Send to agent stays disabled, and the Agent tab reads: Check topics in the Outline to preview what the agent will receive.
examples: Tick The storm scene and Names to keep. Leave The lamp oil empty.
Clear every circle and Send to agent stays disabled.

steps.title: Open the Agent tab.
steps.text: In the sidebar, choose Agent, beside Session, Feedback, and Stores. Destination is at the top of that tab. Send to agent follows it.
examples: Open Agent, beside Session, Feedback, and Stores. The tooltip reads: Hand the selected session to an agent.

steps.title: Pick an Agent.
steps.text: Open the Agent menu and choose who should receive the topics. The status line starts with that name, or reads not configured when nothing resolves.
examples: Choose Claude Code. The status line on the Agent tab starts with that name, then lighthouse-book, then default model.
If nothing resolves, that same line reads not configured.

steps.title: Pick a Project.
steps.text: Open the Project menu and choose the folder the agent should work in, from Recent, All projects, or Add folder…. The middle of the status line should name that folder.
examples: Choose lighthouse-book from Recent. It shows 2 h ago because the manuscript was open then.
field-notes is also on the poster at the top of this page. It is research, so it is the wrong folder.
If lighthouse-book is missing, Add folder… selects it. The middle of the status line should then read lighthouse-book.

steps.title: Leave Model alone, or choose one.
steps.text: Model stays on Agent default until the agent has reported its own list. The status line then ends in default model, so the agent picks for itself.
examples: Leave Model on Agent default. The status line ends in default model, and Claude Code chooses.
Open the menu later only if you want a smaller model for a second pass on the same two topics.

steps.title: Add an instruction, if you like.
steps.text: On the Agent tab, the Optional instruction box is where you say what to do with the topics. Leave it empty and only the checked topics are sent.
examples: The box on the Agent tab names chapters/04-the-storm.md and forbids a new character. The two topics do not say either of those things.
Leave the box empty and both topics still go, with no file to create.

steps.title: Press Send to agent.
steps.text: Nothing is handed over until this press. Read the topics caption on the Agent tab first, and treat that line as the confirmation.
examples: The caption reads: 2 topics will be sent as one prompt turn. Press Send to agent only after you see that line. The next section is the message that press builds.

sections.heading: The message

paragraphs.text: With a session manager, that press builds one prompt. SpeakWith opens with a lead line, your instruction follows, then each checked topic under its own heading.

sections.figureAlt: The prompt handed to Claude Code. It opens with the SpeakWith lead line, then the instruction to write chapter 4 as chapters/04-the-storm.md, then The storm scene and Names to keep. Names to keep says the keeper is Mara Voss and the supply boat is Cormorant.

sections.heading: The terminal

paragraphs.text: Open a session opens this window on lighthouse-book. Claude Code runs the prompt from the section above and writes chapters/04-the-storm.md in that folder.

sections.figureAlt: A terminal window titled lighthouse-book, Claude Code. It is running the SpeakWith prompt, then shows Wrote chapters/04-the-storm.md. The file contains the storm scene and the keeper Mara Voss, taken from the notes.

sections.heading: Rows you may or may not see

paragraphs.text: Two more rows appear under Destination only when there is a choice to make.

steps.title: Terminal.
steps.text: This row is there only when this Mac has more than one terminal app. Choose which one should open.
examples: This job needs a window you can watch. With one terminal app installed, Destination has no Terminal row, and that app is the one that opens on lighthouse-book.
With two terminal apps installed, pick the one that should show Claude Code creating chapters/04-the-storm.md.

steps.title: Runs in.
steps.text: You see Runs in only for SpeakWith's own bridge. Open a session watches a terminal window; Answer here puts the reply on the Agent tab.
examples: Choose Open a session. The terminal figure is Claude Code writing the chapter in lighthouse-book.
Answer here would put the draft on the Agent tab instead. On that path SpeakWith declines a request to create chapters/04-the-storm.md.

steps.title: With your session manager chosen.
steps.text: A second press on the same topics is held: the Agent tab says they were already sent, and Send again repeats them. The Sent ledger, lower on that tab, keeps the list.
examples: Three minutes later the same two topics are still checked. The Agent tab reads: Already sent 3 minutes ago. Send again is what would hand chapter 4 over a second time.
The Sent ledger, lower on the Agent tab, lists that send. Before the first press it read: Nothing sent yet from this tab.

steps.title: With any other agent chosen.
steps.text: Every press is a fresh message, with no hold. The Outline checkboxes are still what gets sent.
examples: This job used the session manager, so the hold above applies. An agent that is not that manager does not hold.
On that other path, a second press sends The storm scene and Names to keep again. Uncheck Names to keep first if the repeat should carry only the scene.

sections.heading: Point SpeakWith at a program of your own

paragraphs.text: Skip this section when Claude Code is already in the Agent menu. When the agent that should write the chapter is missing from that menu, Settings, under Agent, holds the three rows for a program of your own: Agent program, Arguments, and Project folder. How such a program fills the Project menu and the Model menu is on its own page.

sections.linkLabel: Read how a program fills the Project and Model lists.

sections.heading: What the agent can and cannot do

paragraphs.text: In this job you chose Open a session, so Claude Code runs in a terminal in lighthouse-book and writes the chapter there. Answer here is the other choice: the draft comes back onto the Agent tab, and SpeakWith declines a request, made through that connection, to change files on the Mac.

seeAlso.label: See also: Project and model lists, how a program of your own fills the Project menu and the Model menu.

outline.heading: Draft by voice, arrange afterwards
outline.intro: You do not have to know where everything goes before you start talking. Record each idea as it comes, in any order. Every recording lands in the day document as its own section, and the Outline lets you drag those sections into the order the document needs, nested where they belong. The words stay exactly what you said, and the result is plain markdown, so the draft is already in a form every editor can open. This page shows the two moves a drag can make, an indent and a reorder, each as a before and after of the same five recordings.
outline.diagramAlt: SpeakWith Outline poster. The wordmark is at the top right and on each figure. Two before and after figures of the same five recorded text blocks. Each block shows a recorded time, a short heading, and one or two lines of spoken words. A curved arrow runs from the moved block on the left to its new place on the right. Figure 1: the second recording is nested one step under the first, a dashed outline marks where it sat, and the order is unchanged. Figure 2: the fifth recording has moved up between the second and the third, and nothing is indented. The words are the same on both sides.

captions.label: Figure 1. Indent.
captions.text: The second recording is nested under the first. The spoken order is unchanged, and so is every time.

captions.label: Figure 2. Reorder.
captions.text: The fifth recording moves up between the second and the third. Nothing is indented.

paragraphs.text: Spoken ideas arrive in time order. A finished document is in topic order. The Outline is the bridge between the two: every row is one recording, with the time you started speaking and the words you said, and a drag changes neither. It changes only where the recording sits in the day document: under another recording, or earlier or later in the day. Keep each recording to one idea and you will have more to arrange.

Drop a row toward the right edge of the row above it and it nests one step under that row. Figure 1 nests the second recording under the first. The spoken order is unchanged, and so is every time. A row nests one step at a time; a drop that would skip a level is refused.

Drop a row between two others and it moves there, still at the same level. Figure 2 moves the fifth recording up between the second and the third. Nothing is indented. The day document keeps a recording's time marker only where the times still read in order, so a recording moved ahead of earlier ones drops its marker there. The words are untouched.

A drop is a preview. The Outline shows the new arrangement at once, but nothing on disk changes until you press Apply, which writes the arrangement to the day document. Undo takes back the last drag. Drops you never apply change nothing.

seeAlso.label: See also: Send to agent, which takes the Outline rows you have checked to a coding agent on your Mac.

contextAwareInsertion.heading: How typed-in words find their spacing
contextAwareInsertion.intro: A phrase typed into another app sometimes lands with no space before it, or with two. SpeakWith avoids both by looking at the two characters around the cursor before it types, and this page explains that look: what it reads, what it decides, and the six ways a field can answer, from a field that reports everything to one that collapses spacing after the fact.
contextAwareInsertion.diagramAlt: SpeakWith poster in two figures. Figure A, what it looks at: four rows, each a text field with a cursor, the same spoken word, and the result. The one character before the cursor and the one after it are circled and joined by thin leader lines to a label that reads one before, one after. Row one, cursor after a word: one space is added. Row two, cursor after a space: no space is added. Row three, cursor before a period: the word goes in with no space on either side. Row four, a selected word: the spoken word replaces it and the spacing comes from the characters outside the selection. Figure B, when the field will not say: four panels. Legible, Opaque, and Silent each show two phrases landing in the same field with the spacing each kind of field gets. Trimming shows a leading space pasted and eaten, then the same space typed as a keystroke and kept.

captions.label: Figure A. What it looks at.
captions.text: One character before the cursor, one after. Against a word, one space. Against a space, an edge, or closing punctuation, none. A selection is read from its outside.

captions.label: Figure B. When the field will not say.
captions.text: A legible field gets the full rule. An opaque or silent field gets start-of-field spacing plus the join space between phrases. A trimming field keeps its space because the space is typed, not pasted.

paragraphs.text: Before SpeakWith types a finished phrase, it asks the app in front for two characters: the one immediately before the cursor and the one immediately after. Nothing else is read. From those two it decides the spacing, and the rule is short. If the character before is part of a word, the phrase gets one space in front. If it is a space, nothing is added. If there is nothing before the cursor at all, nothing is added either. The same applies after the phrase: one space if a word follows, none if a space or closing punctuation follows, so a phrase typed in front of a period sits snugly against it.

Two details matter more than they look. First, the start of a field and a field that could not be read are treated the same way, on purpose: in both cases SpeakWith adds nothing in front and lets the phrase itself carry its spacing, so a read that fails never turns into a stray space. Second, a hyphen or an underscore before the cursor counts as already joined, so a field that ends in well- gets well-known, not well- known. If you select a word before you speak, the phrase replaces the selection and the two characters are read from outside it, as Figure A shows in its last row.

sections.heading: Why it is one space, never two

paragraphs.text: With Punctuation off, each phrase SpeakWith types ends in one space, so consecutive phrases read as running prose. That join space exists because, for a long time, typing into another app could not see the field at all. When the field can be read, the join space is dropped and the two-character rule decides instead, since keeping both would put two spaces at the seam. When the field cannot be read, the join space is kept, and the next phrase lands after it exactly as it always did. With Punctuation on, your spoken periods and question marks do the separating, and no join space is added.

Every app answers the two-character question in its own way, and the answer, not the app, decides what SpeakWith does. There are six kinds. The first three cover how a field reports its text, the next two cover how it accepts text, and the last one is out of reach.
Legible. The field reports its text and the cursor honestly. The phrase gets the full rule: one space against a word, none against a space or an edge, and the spacing is right on both sides.

Opaque. The field answers, but reports no text at all. An empty answer is just as likely to be an editor that hides its contents as a field that is actually empty, and the two are indistinguishable, so SpeakWith deliberately treats this as unreadable. Believing it would drop the join space and glue phrases together. The phrase lands with no space in front and the join space after, so prose still separates, and as soon as the field shows any text the next phrase gets the full rule. The first phrase into a field that reports nothing can still land against a word with no space.

Silent. The field does not answer, because it has no text to report or because the app is busy. SpeakWith uses the same fallback as an opaque field. Your words are never dropped for want of an answer.

Write-shy. The field reports its cursor but refuses a direct write. SpeakWith re-reads the field after each attempt. If the text is unchanged, it falls back to the clipboard and a paste. If it cannot tell what happened, it stops and says so rather than pasting twice.

Trimming. The field accepts the paste but strips the leading space from pasted text, so phrases run together even though the read was honest. SpeakWith types the one leading space as a keystroke and pastes the rest. A keystroke is not pasted text, so no trimming applies to it, and in a field that keeps leading spaces the result is identical.

Normalizing. The field collapses whitespace later, usually when a message is sent. Spacing that was right at the moment of typing is rewritten afterwards by the app. No way of inserting text can change this; the words still arrive, and the app decides how they are spaced on the way out.

sections.heading: What it reads, and what it never reads

paragraphs.text: The read is two characters, the one before the insertion point and the one after. SpeakWith does not read the document, the rest of the field, or what was on the clipboard before. When a phrase has to go through the clipboard, it is flagged so clipboard managers skip it, and the clipboard is put back afterwards if nothing else wrote to it in the meantime. A password field is detected before anything is written, and SpeakWith refuses to type into it, so a password never passes through the clipboard.

Typing into other apps is a feature of the direct Mac build. The App Store build is sandboxed, and macOS does not allow a sandboxed app to type into another one, so none of this page applies there. Your day document receives every phrase either way.

seeAlso.label: See also: Reading live transcript corrections, for the marks SpeakWith puts on a settled line in its own window.

agentLists.heading: Project and model lists
agentLists.intro: On the Agent tab of SpeakWith from Gumroad, Destination has three menus: Agent, Project, and Model. SpeakWith does not go looking for folders or models on its own. A program on your Mac tells it what to list, over one local address, and this page shows what that program sends. It is written for people who write such a program. If you only use the Agent tab, the Send to agent guide is the page to read.

paragraphs.text: The Engine that ships with SpeakWith from Gumroad keeps a small catalog service at http://127.0.0.1:9896. It starts with the Engine and stays up when you close the SpeakWith window, so a list pushed while the window is closed is there when it opens again. The service listens on this Mac only. Nothing on this page leaves the machine.

Check that it is listening before you write anything:

curl http://127.0.0.1:9896/health

The answer is {"ok":true,"role":"agent_catalog"}. Anything else means the Engine is not running, and every call on this page needs it. Start the Engine and try again.
The Project menu is filled by one call. It replaces the list you sent last time with the one you send now, so send everything you want listed, every time.

Send the folders you know, whole, under a name of your own as the publisher:

curl -X PUT http://127.0.0.1:9896/catalog/menus \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "v": 1,
    "publisher": "my-session-manager",
    "projects": [
      {
        "id": "lighthouse-book",
        "path": "/Users/you/Writing/lighthouse-book",
        "label": "lighthouse-book",
        "last": 1790720000,
        "section": "recent"
      },
      {
        "id": "field-notes",
        "path": "/Users/you/Research/field-notes",
        "label": "field-notes",
        "section": "other"
      }
    ]
  }'

Each row has an id, a path, and a label. The label is the text in the menu. Two fields are optional: last is the Unix time, in seconds, the folder was last worked in, and section is recent or other.

What you see on the Agent tab: rows marked recent, with a last time, appear under Recent, each with how long ago that was, such as 2 h ago. Every other row appears under All projects. When nothing was picked before, the first row is picked for you. A pick that is still in the new list stays picked.
A folder someone adds from the app, through Add folder… under Project, is not yours to replace.

SpeakWith sends that folder as one call of its own and marks the row manual, so your next menus push leaves it in the list. You can make the same call yourself. The folder has to exist on this Mac.

curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:9896/catalog/projects \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{ "path": "/Users/you/Writing/lighthouse-book", "label": "lighthouse-book" }'

The menus push replaces your projects and your own model rows. If you send destinations, it replaces those as a whole. It does not touch model rows another agent advertised, and it never changes a pick that is still a row.

The Model menu reads Agent default until some list arrives. There are two ways to hand one over. Use the first when your program is the one filling the Project menu anyway. Use the second when your program is the agent itself, connected over ACP.
On the same menus push.

Add a models list to the menus push above. Each row has an id, the value your program understands when the pick is handed back, and a label, the text in the menu. A description is optional.

"models": [
  { "id": "claude-opus-5-5", "label": "Opus 5.5" },
  { "id": "claude-sonnet-5-5", "label": "Sonnet 5.5", "description": "Faster, for a second pass" }
]

Rows sent this way are filed under your publisher. Your next push replaces them and leaves the rows other agents advertised alone.
On session/new.

An agent connected over ACP answers session/new. Put the models in that answer as a configOptions entry whose category is model. SpeakWith reads it and stores the list under that agent with PUT /catalog/models/{agent}. Your program never calls the catalog for models at all.

{
  "sessionId": "s-1",
  "configOptions": [
    {
      "id": "model",
      "category": "model",
      "currentValue": "claude-opus-5-5",
      "options": [
        { "value": "claude-opus-5-5", "name": "Opus 5.5", "description": "Most capable" },
        { "value": "claude-sonnet-5-5", "name": "Sonnet 5.5" }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

Each value becomes the model id and each name the label; leave name out and the value is shown. currentValue names the row the agent is on right now. SpeakWith also reads the older models.availableModels shape, but when an answer carries both, the configOptions entry wins.

What you see on the Agent tab: with the first way, the Model menu fills as soon as your push lands, before any agent has been contacted. With the second, it fills once that agent has answered session/new, which happens when a session is opened with it. Either way the status line ends in default model until someone picks a row, and a pick that is still in the list stays picked across pushes.

Every write answers with the whole catalog as it now stands, so you never need a second call to see what your change settled to. You can also read it at any time, and the answer includes the current pick as selection, with agent, projectPath, and modelId:

curl http://127.0.0.1:9896/catalog

To be told when something changes, open http://127.0.0.1:9896/events. It is a server-sent event stream with one catalog event per change. The event carries no detail; read the catalog again when it arrives.

privacy.heading: Privacy Policy
privacy.intro: SpeakWith is built around a simple principle: your words are yours. This policy explains what SpeakWith does and does not do with the recordings, transcripts, and documents you create.

sections.heading: Your recordings are processed on your device

paragraphs.text: SpeakWith records, transcribes, organises, and searches entirely on your own device, whether that is your Mac or your iOS device. Turning speech into text, shaping it into your daily document, and answering your searches all happen locally. SpeakWith does not need an internet connection to do its core work, and it does not send your recordings to a server to be processed.

Two optional features can send transcript text, never audio, to a language model: generating a session title and checking corrections. Both are off until you turn them on. Session titles can use your OpenAI API key or a local Ollama model on your Mac, so nothing leaves your machine when you choose Ollama. Correction checks, if you enable them, use your OpenAI key.

sections.heading: No telemetry, analytics, or tracking in the app

paragraphs.text: The SpeakWith application does not include usage analytics, advertising, or behavioural tracking. We do not collect a record of how you use the app, what you record, or what you search for. There are no third-party trackers in the application.

This is a statement about the app itself. This website, which is separate software running in your browser, measures anonymous visitor counts; that is described under “The support website” below. Nothing measured on the website is connected to the app, and the app never reports anything to us.

Everything SpeakWith produces (your recordings, transcripts, and daily documents) is stored as ordinary files on your device. You can open, copy, move, back up, and delete them with any tool you like. They are not locked inside a proprietary store, and they are not held in an account that we control.

If something in SpeakWith goes wrong, a diagnostic report can help us fix it. SpeakWith never sends such a report automatically. Crash and diagnostic reporting is strictly opt-in: nothing leaves your device unless you explicitly choose to send it, and you can decline or turn it off at any time.

This website uses TelemetryDeck, a privacy-focused analytics service, to count page views and how often the download and pricing links are used. It tells us which pages people find useful. It is not used to profile you.

No cookies are set for analytics and no advertising or cross-site tracking identifiers are used. Visits are identified only by a random value that lives in your browser tab and is discarded when you close it, and TelemetryDeck anonymises that value before storing it. We see aggregate counts — pages, referrers, campaign links, browser and country — never individual visitors, and never anything you type.
Standard server request logs may exist at the hosting provider, as they do for any website.
If this policy changes, the updated version will be posted here with a new date. Material changes will be summarised at the top of the page.
Questions about privacy? Reach us through the support channels listed with the app.
